voyages.name: The crossing to Sahul
rows: 70–90 km, out of sight of land
voyages.text:
The first crossing anyone made that could not be seen across. Even at the lowest sea level of the glacial cycle there were 70–90 km of open water between Timor and Sahul, and the target could not be seen from the departure point.

**No boat survives.** The evidence is the arrival. What the record does support is a negative: experimental crossings found bamboo rafts made under a knot against the Kuroshio and failed outright, while a 7.6 m cedar dugout crossed 225 km of open water in 45 hours. If the craft was anything, it was more like a dugout than a raft.
voyages.cite: Clarkson et al., *Nature* (2017); Kaifu experimental crossings, 2016–19.

voyages.name: The Wallacean stepping stones
voyages.text:
Wallacea is why the crossing to Sahul is not one crossing but a dozen. Between the Sunda shelf and the Sahul shelf lies a belt of deep water that no fall in sea level ever bridged, and every island in it had to be reached over open sea.

Those trenches are why the animals on either side are different, and why the people on both sides are not.
voyages.cite: Wallace, *The Malay Archipelago* (1869); Bird et al., *Sci. Rep.* (2019).

voyages.name: The obsidian run to Kozushima
voyages.text:
Kozushima is 50 km off the Izu coast and has been an island for the whole of human occupation of Japan. Obsidian from it is found on the mainland in layers around 38,000 years old.

That is the evidence: not a boat, not a picture of a boat, but a stone that could only have arrived by sea, repeatedly, for thousands of years. A single drift accounts for one flake. It does not account for a trade.
voyages.cite: Ikeya, *Quaternary International* (2015).

voyages.name: North along the Ryukyus
voyages.text:
A chain of islands, each just visible from the last except where it is not. The gap from Taiwan to Yonaguni is 110 km across the Kuroshio, one of the fastest currents in any ocean, and Yonaguni cannot be seen from sea level at Taiwan.

The crossing was rebuilt and paddled in 2019 in a cedar dugout: 45 hours, no sight of the target for most of it, and a landfall made by aiming deliberately upstream of it.
voyages.cite: Kaifu et al., experimental crossings, 2016-2019.

voyages.name: The cedar run to Egypt
voyages.text:
Egypt had no timber worth a hull and Lebanon had little else. The trade is old enough that the Egyptian word for a seagoing ship is *kbnt* - a Byblos ship - and Snefru's annals record forty vessels of cedar arriving in a single year.

A state that cannot grow its own masts must be able to reach the place that can. It is one of the oldest reasons for a navy.
voyages.cite: Palermo Stone, reign of Snefru; Marcus, *Aegypten und Levante* (2002).

voyages.name: Dilmun to Meluhha
voyages.text:
Mesopotamian tablets name three places downriver: Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha. Dilmun is Bahrain, Magan is Oman, and Meluhha is almost certainly the Indus. The tablets are receipts - copper by weight, carnelian by the bead - which makes this the earliest sea trade anyone can put numbers to.

Indus weights and seals turn up in Mesopotamia, and Mesopotamian goods in Indus ports.
voyages.cite: Ratnagar, *Trading Encounters* (2004).

voyages.name: Hatshepsut's fleet to Punt
rows: incense trees, ebony, ivory, live baboons
voyages.text:
The Deir el-Bahri reliefs show five ships, their cargo and their crews, and are the earliest detailed picture anyone has of a seagoing fleet. Timbers and rigging of the same era were excavated at Wadi Gawasis on the Red Sea coast - cedar planks, mortise-and-tenon joints, and the anchors.

The ships were built inland, carried in pieces to the coast and assembled there, which is why the reliefs also show them being taken apart.
voyages.cite: Naville, *The Temple of Deir el Bahari*; Bard & Fattovich, Wadi Gawasis.

voyages.name: The Uluburun ship's last voyage
voyages.text:
She sank off Kas with everything aboard, which is why she is worth more than any ship that survived. Ten tonnes of Cypriot copper in oxhide ingots, a tonne of tin - the exact ratio for bronze - glass, ebony, ivory, Baltic amber and a gold scarab of Nefertiti.

Cargo from at least eleven cultures in one hull. The Bronze Age Mediterranean was not a set of coastal trades but one system, and the proof of it lies on a slope at 44 metres.
voyages.cite: Pulak, *IJNA* (1998); Institute of Nautical Archaeology.

voyages.name: The Austronesian expansion
rows: a third of the surface of the planet
largely INTO the prevailing trade winds
double hull, crab-claw sail, lashed-lug planking, no metal
about 75° made good — poor, and positive
voyages.text:
The largest maritime expansion in human history, and it went **the wrong way for the wind**. The trades in the tropical Pacific blow from the east; the settlement runs west to east.

That is only possible with a rig that generates lift rather than merely catching wind. A crab claw on a double hull makes good about 75° to the true wind — poor by modern standards, and the crucial thing is that it is *positive*, where a square rig in the same conditions makes none at all. Sailing upwind also means you can always run home if you find nothing, which is how you explore an ocean and survive.

The East Polynesian dates are far younger than once thought: the short chronology moved Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and New Zealand several centuries later.
voyages.cite: Irwin, *Archaeology in Oceania* 58 (2023); Wilmshurst et al. (2011).

voyages.name: Africa circumnavigated, or claimed
rows: the sun on the right hand
voyages.text:
Herodotus reports that Phoenicians sent by Necho II sailed from the Red Sea and returned through the Pillars of Heracles three years later, stopping each year to sow a crop and wait for the harvest.

He adds that they claimed the sun was on their right hand as they rounded the south of Africa, and says he does not believe it. That detail is why modern readers do: sailing west round the Cape, the noon sun is to the north, and it is not something a fabricator in the Mediterranean would invent.
voyages.cite: Herodotus IV.42.

voyages.name: Hanno down the Guinea coast
voyages.text:
The *Periplus of Hanno* is a Greek translation of a Punic inscription, and it reads like a log: islands counted, rivers named, a coast that burns at night, and a mountain of fire the crew called the Chariot of the Gods.

West African grass fires and Mount Cameroon both fit. Punic material has been excavated at Mogador, which is as far as the text can be checked.
voyages.cite: *Periplus of Hanno*; Warmington, *Carthage*.

voyages.name: The Athenian armada to Syracuse
voyages.text:
A hundred and thirty-four triremes, none of which could carry a day's water. A trireme is a racing hull with two hundred men in it and no hold: it beaches every night, and the fleet's range is the distance between friendly beaches.

That is the whole story of the expedition. Athens could reach Sicily and could not feed itself once there, and two years later the fleet was gone and the crews were in the quarries.
voyages.cite: Thucydides VI-VII; Morrison & Coates, *The Athenian Trireme*.

voyages.name: The monsoon crossing
rows: November to January, on the north-east monsoon
voyages.text:
The only wind system on Earth that reverses, and it fixes the sailing calendar of half the world. The *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* names the month outright — 'about the month of July, that is Epiphi' — four separate times for four separate routes.

In this ocean the departure **date** is not a free variable. Miss the monsoon and you wait six months.
voyages.cite: *Periplus Maris Erythraei* §§14, 39, 49, 56.

voyages.name: Berenike to Barygaza on the monsoon
voyages.text:
The *Periplus of the Erythraean Sea* is a merchant's handbook, and its most valuable sentence credits Hippalus with using the south-west monsoon to cross open ocean instead of following the coast.

That halves the voyage and doubles the risk, and it turns a coasting trade into a scheduled one: leave in July, arrive in September, wait for the north-east monsoon and come home. Roman coin hoards in southern India are the receipts.
voyages.cite: *Periplus Maris Erythraei*; Casson (ed., 1989).

voyages.name: The Alexandria grain fleet
voyages.text:
Rome ate Egypt. A million people were fed on grain that had to cross 1,900 km of sea, and the fleet that did it sailed under state contract, because a city that runs out of bread stops being governable.

The route out was easy and the route home was against the etesian winds, which is why the ships went north about Crete - and why Paul's grain ship, on that same route, ended up on Malta.
voyages.cite: Acts 27; Casson, *Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World*.

voyages.name: The Han coast to Rinan
voyages.text:
The southern edge of the Han empire was reached by sea, and the commandery of Rinan sat at the far end of it. From there Chinese records log an embassy claiming to come from Daqin - Rome - in AD 166.

Whether they were envoys or merchants saying what would get them an audience, they arrived by ship, and the two ends of Eurasia were in contact by sea before either had a name for the other that the other recognised.
voyages.cite: *Hou Hanshu*, Chapter 88.

voyages.name: The Srivijaya straits
voyages.text:
Every ship between China and India went through one of two straits, and Srivijaya held both. That is the entire basis of the state: not territory, but a chokepoint and a fleet able to compel ships into its harbour.

A Chinese pilgrim stopped there for six months in 671 to learn Sanskrit before going on to India, which tells you it was also a place where you waited - for the monsoon, and for permission.
voyages.cite: Yijing, *Record of Buddhist Practices*; Wolters, *Early Indonesian Commerce*.

voyages.name: The Norse Atlantic
rows: 1021 CE exactly — from a cosmic-ray spike in the wood
clinker-built, one square sail, shallow draught
latitude sailing along a parallel; no instruments
voyages.text:
Crossing an ocean without being able to fix a position, in an open boat, by holding a latitude and running west.

The Vinland date is one of the most precise in archaeology: a cosmic-ray event in 993 CE left a spike in tree rings worldwide, and wood cut at L'Anse aux Meadows shows exactly 28 rings after it. **1021 CE**, to the year.
voyages.cite: Kuitems et al., *Nature* (2021); Viking Ship Museum, Roskilde.

voyages.name: Greenland to Vinland
voyages.text:
The sagas describe three landfalls west of Greenland, and one of them has been excavated: eight turf buildings at the northern tip of Newfoundland, with a smithy, iron boat rivets and a spindle whorl.

A cut branch from the site was dated by a solar storm of known year to AD 1021 - the first exact date for Europeans in the Americas, four hundred and seventy-one years early.
voyages.cite: Ingstad excavations; Kuitems et al., *Nature* (2021).

voyages.name: Quanzhou to Calicut
voyages.text:
A Song junk had watertight bulkheads, a stern-mounted rudder, a compass and a hull that could take the ground - everything Europe would spend four centuries acquiring. The Quanzhou wreck raised in 1974 had thirteen sealed compartments.

The bulkhead is the whole argument: hole one compartment and you lose one compartment. It is a structural idea, and it came from looking at a bamboo stem.
voyages.cite: Quanzhou ship, 1974; Needham, *Science and Civilisation in China* IV.3.

voyages.name: Hawaiki to Aotearoa
voyages.text:
The last large habitable landmass on Earth to be reached by people, and it was reached upwind, deliberately, in double-hulled canoes carrying taro, kumara, dogs and rats.

Radiocarbon on the commensal package puts arrival around 1280 - not a slow leak of castaways but a short, decisive settlement, which is what you would expect of a voyage planned to be repeatable.
voyages.cite: Wilmshurst et al., *PNAS* (2011).

voyages.name: The dhow road to Kilwa
voyages.text:
Ibn Battuta sailed this coast and thought Kilwa one of the finest cities in the world. It was built on gold that came overland to Sofala and then north by sea, and it minted its own coin - since found on a beach in northern Australia and in the Persian Gulf.

The rhythm is the monsoon: down with the north-east from November, home with the south-west from April, and no choice about either.
voyages.cite: Ibn Battuta, *Rihla*; Chittick, *Kilwa* (1974).

voyages.name: The Hanse run to Bergen
voyages.text:
The cog is a box with a mast: flat-bottomed, clinker-built, one square sail, a stern rudder. It sails badly and carries enormously, which is the right trade for a sea you cross in short hops with salt one way and dried cod the other.

The Bryggen quarter at Bergen was a Hanseatic enclave with its own law. Salt from Lueneburg went north, stockfish came south, and the League's leverage was that it held both halves.
voyages.cite: Bremen cog, 1962; Dollinger, *The German Hansa*.

voyages.name: Zheng He's treasure fleets
voyages.text:
Seven voyages across the Indian Ocean, sixty years before a Portuguese ship reached it — and then the archives were destroyed and the fleets were never rebuilt.

**The famous dimensions come from fiction.** The 44-*zhang* figure first appears in Luo Maodeng's *Xiyang Ji* of 1597, a novel in which ships are built with divine help, and was carried into the official history in 1739. The Longjiang shipyard was excavated in 2003–04 and its largest building basin is 41 m wide, against a claimed 52 m beam. The hull drawn here is at the defensible length.
voyages.cite: Church, *Monumenta Serica* 53 (2005); Longjiang shipyard excavation, 2003–04.

voyages.name: Dias to the Cape
rows: the Great Fish River, by the crew's demand
voyages.text:
Dias found the Cape by being blown past it. Held off the coast for thirteen days in a southerly gale, he ran east when it eased and made no land - then turned north and struck a coast running east to west instead of north to south.

That accident is the sailing instruction for the next four hundred years: do not follow the African coast south, stand out into the Atlantic and let the westerlies bring you round.
voyages.cite: Barros, *Decadas da Asia*; Ravenstein (1900).

voyages.name: Columbus's first crossing
voyages.text:
He was wrong about the size of the Earth by a quarter and wrong about the position of Asia by a hemisphere, and the two errors together produced a distance he was willing to sail.

What he had right was the wind. Out on the north-east trades from the Canaries, home on the westerlies from the latitude of the Azores - the *volta do mar*, learned by the Portuguese in the Atlantic islands. That loop, not the landfall, is the transferable discovery.
voyages.cite: *Diario* of the first voyage (Las Casas abstract).

voyages.name: Da Gama to India

legs.name: the great arc — reconstructed; no longitude was ever logged

rows: 30 on the return crossing; as many again before
voyages.text:
The *volta do mar*, at full scale. Rather than creep down the African coast against the wind and current, da Gama stood **west and south into the empty Atlantic**, swung round the South Atlantic high, and came in on the westerlies below the Cape: **93 days and 5,180 nautical miles** from Cape Verde to a landfall at about 30°S.

It is the longest open-ocean passage anyone had deliberately made, and it was a wind-field calculation. Sailing away from your destination in order to reach it is the first great piece of applied knowledge about the ocean.

**The arc drawn here is a reconstruction.** The journal records a heading and a date and never once a longitude, so where the fleet actually turned is not known — only that it was somewhere in the western South Atlantic.

**The pilot taken on at Malindi was not Ibn Majid.** The journal calls him only 'a Christian pilot' — the Portuguese routinely mistook Hindus for Christians — and the chroniclers call him a Gujarati whose supposed name, *Malemo Cana*, is not a name at all but two titles: *mu'allim*, master, and *kanaka*, his caste. Tibbetts, Subrahmanyam and Khoury all reject the identification; Ibn Majid thought himself too old to navigate by 1498.
voyages.cite: Ravenstein (ed.), *A Journal of the First Voyage of Vasco da Gama* (Hakluyt, 1898); Tibbetts; Subrahmanyam.

voyages.name: Magellan and Elcano

legs.name: Puerto San Julián — the winter, and the mutiny
Cabo Froward — All Saints, and the name

rows: ~35 — 18 in *Victoria*, 12 held at Cape Verde, 3–5 from *Trinidad*
Returned to Spain by any route
98 days; 21 died — 19 crew, a Patagonian, a Brazilian
38 days; 570 km; the narrows are 3.7 km wide
killed at Mactan, 27 April 1521, with a year still to run
voyages.text:
The voyage that measured the planet, and it did so by nearly killing everyone on it. Five ships and about 270 men left; one ship and eighteen men came back.

The Pacific crossing is the part that could not be planned for, because nobody knew how wide it was. **Ninety-eight days without fresh food.** They ate the leather off the yards. That the ocean was that big was the single most important thing the voyage found out.

Magellan himself never completed it — he was killed at Mactan on 27 April 1521, with more than a year still to run. The circumnavigation is Elcano's.

**The mutiny was not an Easter mutiny.** It broke out on the night of 1 April 1520 at Puerto San Julián — which was **Palm Sunday**, not Easter. Julian Easter that year fell on 8 April, which means Quesada was beheaded and quartered on Holy Saturday, the eve of it. The popular framing gets the liturgy exactly one week wrong.

**And they came home a day early.** At Cape Verde the shore party asked what day it was and were told Thursday; the ship's log said Wednesday. Two men had kept independent logs — Pigafetta and the pilot Albo — and neither had missed a day. Sailing west with the sun, they had counted 1,023 days where a man standing still counted 1,024. It is the first empirical proof that the world needs a date line, and nobody had anticipated it.

*The famous 18 is the number aboard* Victoria. *About 35 people actually went round; about 90 got back to Spain, most of them deserters who had turned for home in the strait two years earlier.*
voyages.cite: Pigafetta and Albo's log-book, in Stanley (ed.), Hakluyt Society, 1874; Navarrete's armada accounts.

voyages.name: Drake's circumnavigation
voyages.text:
The second circumnavigation, and the first whose commander came home. It was a raid rather than an expedition: the return to investors was roughly 4,700 per cent, and Elizabeth's share exceeded her ordinary annual revenue.

The navigational content is real, though - the Strait of Magellan westbound, a run north with no chart at all, and a Pacific crossing made because going back the way he came meant sailing past everyone he had robbed.
voyages.cite: *The World Encompassed* (1628); Kelsey, *Sir Francis Drake* (1998).

voyages.name: The Grand Banks cod fleet
voyages.text:
Before there was a colony there was a fishery. Several hundred European vessels a year were working the Banks by the 1570s - Basque, Breton, Portuguese and West Country - and the shore stations that dried the catch were the first sustained European presence in North America.

The fish was the point and the land was a drying rack. Salt cod fed Catholic Europe on 150 fast days a year, which is a market with a calendar.
voyages.cite: Innis, *The Cod Fisheries* (1940); Pope, *Fish into Wine* (2004).

voyages.name: The Manila galleon's return

legs.name: Acapulco, four to six months out

voyages.text:
The same two ports, opposite directions, and half the time or less one way. There is no argument in this whole model that makes the point more cleanly.

Westbound you run down the north-east trades at 13°N and it is easy. Eastbound there is no wind at that latitude that will take you, so you must climb to 40°N, pick up the Kuroshio and the westerlies, cross the widest part of the Pacific, and come down the American coast. Thousands of extra miles, and men arrived dead of scurvy.
voyages.cite: Schurz, *The Manila Galleon*; Urdaneta's *tornaviaje*, 1565.

voyages.name: The treasure fleet home
voyages.text:
Silver from Potosi and Zacatecas moved on a timetable: two fleets a year, assembling at Havana, sailing together through the Florida Strait and up the Gulf Stream before turning east for the Azores.

Convoy is a response to a specific fact - that the wind gives an enemy the same route you are obliged to take. The Spanish lost an entire fleet to it exactly once, at Matanzas in 1628, and kept the system for two centuries.
voyages.cite: Haring, *Trade and Navigation between Spain and the Indies*.

voyages.name: The Brouwer Route to Batavia
rows: a lee shore nobody could locate
voyages.text:
Hendrik Brouwer's instruction of 1611 cut the passage from Europe to Java from over a year to about six months: from the Cape, run east in the forties for a thousand leagues, then turn north for the Sunda Strait.

The cost was that nobody could measure longitude. Turn north too late and you hit Western Australia, which is how the *Batavia* was wrecked in 1629 and how the Dutch charted that coast entirely by accident.
voyages.cite: VOC sailing instructions, 1617; Mutch, *The First Discovery of Australia*.

voyages.name: The fluyt in the Baltic grain trade
rows: levied at the Sound, on deck area
voyages.text:
The *moedernegotie* - the mother trade. The fluyt was designed for it: cheap, lightly built, a huge hold, a narrow deck to cheat the Sound toll, and a crew a third the size of an English ship of the same burden.

It is a purpose-built freighter, and it is why the Dutch could undercut everyone. The design is the business model.
voyages.cite: Unger, *Dutch Shipbuilding before 1800*.

voyages.name: The Middle Passage
voyages.text:
The era's principal Atlantic cargo. Between the sixteenth century and the nineteenth about 12.5 million people were embarked and about 10.7 million landed; the difference is the crossing.

It took six to ten weeks. The ships were built or refitted for it - a slave deck inserted at half height, gratings, a barricade across the waist - and the economics were computed in advance from an assumed mortality. That calculation is the thing to understand about the design.
voyages.cite: Slave Voyages database (Emory); Rediker, *The Slave Ship* (2007).

voyages.name: Cook's first voyage
rows: observe the transit of Venus, then look for a southern continent
Deaths at sea, first two years
about a third of the ship's company, of dysentery and malaria
voyages.text:
A voyage that solved scurvy and was then wrecked by dysentery. Cook lost almost nobody to scurvy in two years at sea — an astonishing result for the period — and then buried about a third of his company after a few weeks refitting at Batavia.

The Barrier Reef grounding on 11 June 1770 nearly ended it: *Endeavour* was held off the bottom by a piece of coral wedged in her own hull.
voyages.cite: Cook, *Journals*, ed. Beaglehole; Royal Museums Greenwich.

voyages.name: Steam crosses the Atlantic
voyages.text:
The moment the wind stopped mattering. *Great Western* crossed westbound — the hard direction, against the prevailing wind that made a sailing packet take forty days — in fifteen days and five hours, and arrived with 200 tons of coal still in her bunkers.

*Sirius* beat her there by hours, having left four days earlier, and the story that her crew burned the furniture is a newspaper invention: they burned four barrels of resin and still had fifteen tons of coal.
voyages.cite: Fox, *The Ocean Railway*; Griffiths, *Steam at Sea*.

voyages.name: The New Bedford whaler to the Japan grounds
voyages.text:
A whaling voyage lasted three to four years and the ship was a factory: try-works amidships, casks in the hold, and a crew paid in shares of a catch that might not happen.

The fleet's charts of the Pacific were better than any navy's, because the whalers went where nobody else had reason to go. Melville shipped out of New Bedford in 1841 and got a book out of it; most got a lay of one two-hundredth.
voyages.cite: Starbuck, *History of the American Whale Fishery*; Melville, *Moby-Dick*.

voyages.name: The emigrant run to Melbourne
rows: great circle, deep in the forties
voyages.text:
Great-circle sailing, argued by Maury from wind and current data rather than from geometry alone, put the emigrant ships deep into the forties and fifties - colder, rougher, and weeks faster.

The *Marco Polo* did Liverpool to Melbourne in 68 days in 1852 and came home in 76. The passengers below decks did not choose the route and were not told what it cost in ice.
voyages.cite: Maury, *Sailing Directions*; Cutler, *Greyhounds of the Sea*.

voyages.name: The guano run from the Chinchas
voyages.text:
Three small islands off Peru held a hundred feet of accumulated seabird droppings, and for thirty years they were the most valuable real estate in the Pacific. Guano was the first industrial fertiliser, and it went round the Horn.

The loading was done by indentured Chinese labourers under conditions that killed a large share of them. Twelve million tonnes were shipped, the islands were stripped, and the trade ended when there was nothing left to load.
voyages.cite: Cushman, *Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World* (2013).

voyages.name: The tea race from Fuzhou
voyages.text:
Sixteen thousand miles from Fuzhou to London, and in 1866 the *Ariel* and the *Taeping* docked on the same tide after ninety-nine days.

The premium for the season's first tea is what paid for hulls that carried less and cost more. Three years later the Suez Canal opened, and the logic of a fast sailing hull on a long route stopped making money.
voyages.cite: MacGregor, *The Tea Clippers*.

voyages.name: The Great Eastern lays the cable
voyages.text:
She was six times the tonnage of any ship afloat, a commercial disaster as a liner, and the only hull in the world that could hold 4,300 km of cable and pay it out without stopping.

When it worked, in July 1866, a message between London and New York went from ten days to a few minutes. Then they went back, grappled up the cable lost the previous year from 3,700 m, spliced it, and landed a second one.
voyages.cite: Field, *History of the Atlantic Telegraph*; Dugan, *The Great Iron Ship*.

voyages.name: P&O to Bombay through the canal
voyages.text:
The canal is a hundred and ninety-three kilometres long and it removed six thousand from the voyage to India. It also removed the sailing ship from the route: there is no wind in a ditch, and a hull that must be towed for a day has lost its advantage.

Steam and Suez arrive together and are the same event. The route reverts to the one the Romans used, and the Cape becomes a detour again.
voyages.cite: Suez Canal Company records; Fletcher, *Journal of Modern History* (1958).

voyages.name: The wool clipper's run home
rows: 363 nautical miles — 15.1 knots averaged for 24 hours
the westerlies blow round the world unbroken below 40°S
voyages.text:
The last thing sail was still best at. The Suez Canal killed the tea trade for sailing ships in 1869 — there is no wind in a cut — so the clippers were driven onto the routes the canal did not help, and the Australian wool run was the best of them.

It is a route that only makes sense if you read the wind: you do not sail back the way you came. You run east, all the way round the bottom of the world, on the only belt of wind on Earth that has no land in its way.
voyages.cite: Royal Museums Greenwich; Lubbock, *The Colonial Clippers*.

voyages.name: The Baltic Fleet's last voyage

legs.name: Dogger Bank — they fire on trawlers
Nosy Be — two months at anchor

rows: six battleships sunk in an afternoon
voyages.text:
A fleet sailed two-thirds of the way round the world because it had no bases along the route, and was destroyed in an afternoon by one that was six knots faster and could see further.

Coal is the whole story. Without a friendly port anywhere on the way, every ton had to come from chartered German colliers, and the squadron was tied to the speed of its slowest transports. This is what the age of steam did: it freed ships from the wind and chained them to fuel.
voyages.cite: Corbett, *Maritime Operations in the Russo-Japanese War*.

voyages.name: The Preussen on the nitrate run
voyages.text:
The only five-masted full-rigged ship ever built: 5,081 tonnes of steel with no engine at all, carrying coal out and Chilean nitrate home round the Horn.

She was not a survival. She was faster and cheaper than steam on that particular route, because a sailing ship burns nothing on a passage where coal has to be bought at both ends. A Channel steamer ran her down in 1910, which is a fair summary of the period.
voyages.cite: Laeisz Line records; Villiers, *The Way of a Ship*.

voyages.name: Titanic's maiden voyage
voyages.text:
She carried lifeboats for 1,178 people and 2,224 aboard, which was legal: the Board of Trade scaled boats to tonnage, and the rule had not been revised since 1894, when the largest ship afloat was a third her size.

The wireless operators had been told to clear a backlog of passenger traffic. The ice warnings that reached the bridge were not plotted. She went down in two hours and forty minutes, and the international ice patrol exists because of it.
voyages.cite: British Wreck Commissioner's Inquiry (1912); US Senate Inquiry (1912).

voyages.name: The Wyoming in the coal trade
rows: wood, at the limit of it
voyages.text:
The largest wooden ship ever built, 137 m over the spars, six masts, and so long that she worked in a seaway - the hull flexed, the seams opened, and the pumps ran more or less permanently.

Wood had reached its limit and this is what the limit looks like. She foundered with all hands off Nantucket in 1924, most probably from exactly that.
voyages.cite: Snow, *Wyoming*; Baker, *Maritime History of Bath*.

voyages.name: The Grand Fleet to Jutland
voyages.text:
*Dreadnought* made every other battleship obsolete in 1906 - all big guns, turbine drive, twenty-one knots - and set off a building race that both sides then declined to risk in battle.

Jutland is the one afternoon they spent. Two hundred and fifty ships, one inconclusive engagement, heavier British losses, and a German fleet that went home and stayed there. The blockade held, which was the only question that mattered.
voyages.cite: Official Despatches (1920); Massie, *Castles of Steel*.

voyages.name: Convoy HX to Liverpool
voyages.text:
The convoy is a mathematical object. A submarine has to find the ships before it can sink them, and a hundred ships in one formation are barely easier to find than one - so concentration cuts the number of contacts, and the escort is spread over more hulls.

The fight was decided in the mid-ocean air gap, where neither side had land-based cover. Very-long-range Liberators and escort carriers closed it in 1943, and the sinkings stopped almost at once.
voyages.cite: Roskill, *The War at Sea*; Blair, *Hitler's U-Boat War*.

voyages.name: The Kido Butai to Hawai'i
voyages.text:
Six carriers, four thousand kilometres, radio silence, and a route chosen because nobody sails it: the northern Pacific in winter, out of the shipping lanes, fogbound and rough enough to make refuelling marginal.

They launched 353 aircraft from 230 nautical miles. The battleships were in harbour and the carriers were not, which is the sentence the next four years turn on.
voyages.cite: Prange, *At Dawn We Slept*; Japanese Monograph No. 97.

voyages.name: Yamato's last sortie
voyages.text:
The largest battleship ever built, sailing with fuel for a one-way passage and orders to beach herself off Okinawa and fire until destroyed. She was sighted at once and attacked by 386 aircraft.

Two hours, ten torpedoes, seven bombs, and 3,055 of 3,332 men. Her nine 46 cm guns, the largest ever mounted at sea, never fired at a ship in the whole war. The aircraft carrier had already settled the question she was built to answer.
voyages.cite: Japanese naval war diary; Skulski, *The Battleship Yamato*.

voyages.name: Ideal-X, the first box voyage
voyages.text:
Fifty-eight boxes on the deck of a converted T-2 tanker, Newark to Houston, 26 April 1956. Malcom McLean was a trucking man, and his insight was not the box but the fact that the box need never be unpacked.

Break-bulk loading cost about $5.86 a tonne. Containerised, it cost 16 cents. Nearly everything about where things are made follows from that ratio.
voyages.cite: Levinson, *The Box* (2006).

voyages.name: Shenzhen to New York through Panama
voyages.text:
The 2016 locks doubled the maximum ship: 366 m long, 51.25 m beam, 14,000 TEU instead of 5,000. That single dimension redrew the east coast of the United States, because a port that cannot take a neo-Panamax loses the traffic to one that can.

Every major Atlantic port dredged. The Bayonne Bridge was raised by 20 m so the ships could pass under it. The canal's width is a specification the whole system is built to.
voyages.cite: Panama Canal Authority; Port Authority of NY & NJ.

voyages.name: The Northern Sea Route
voyages.text:
Fourteen thousand kilometres from Murmansk to Shanghai instead of twenty-one thousand through Suez, and for a few weeks a year it is now open to a strengthened hull without an icebreaker.

It is not a shipping lane yet. There is no rescue within days, no salvage, insurance is punitive, and a schedule that depends on the ice is not a schedule. What has changed is that the question is commercial rather than theoretical.
voyages.cite: Northern Sea Route Administration transit statistics.

voyages.name: Singapore to Rotterdam
voyages.text:
The main line, when it is open. Three chokepoints in one voyage - Malacca, Bab el Mandeb, Suez - each a place where the whole trade between Asia and Europe is a few kilometres wide.

The *Ever Given* demonstrated the consequence in March 2021 by turning sideways: six days aground, 369 ships waiting, and about nine billion dollars a day of trade held up behind one hull.
voyages.cite: Suez Canal Authority; Lloyd's List (2021).

voyages.name: Iron ore, Port Hedland to Qingdao
rows: Capesize - too big for either canal
voyages.text:
The largest bulk trade on Earth by tonnage: about 900 million tonnes a year of iron ore, most of it from one stretch of the Pilbara to one country.

Port Hedland loads a Capesize every few hours. Those ships are named for the Cape because they are too large for Suez or Panama and have to go round - a class of vessel defined entirely by the canals it cannot use.
voyages.cite: Pilbara Ports Authority; UNCTAD.

voyages.name: Asia to Europe, today
rows: lock chambers and dredged channels, not wind
voyages.text:
The last chapter is not about the sea at all. A modern container ship's route is set by **numbers written down by engineers** — the inside dimension of a lock, the depth of a dredged channel — rather than by anything the ocean does.

Panamax is not a ship. It is the inside of a lock built in 1914, and for a century the world's fleet was designed around it. The ocean is still there. It has simply stopped being the thing that decides.
voyages.cite: UNCTAD *Review of Maritime Transport*; Suez Canal Authority; EIA chokepoint data.

voyages.name: Shanghai to Los Angeles
voyages.text:
The busiest deep-sea container lane in the world, and it runs a great circle up past the Aleutians because the Earth is round and the saving is real.

A 14,000-TEU ship on this route carries more cargo than the entire British merchant fleet of 1900. The service is weekly, and the whole system depends on it being a schedule.
voyages.cite: UNCTAD *Review of Maritime Transport*; Port of Los Angeles statistics.

voyages.name: A carrier strike group deploys
voyages.text:
A hundred thousand tonnes, two reactors, no need to refuel for twenty years, and about seventy aircraft. Its purpose is to put a working airfield within range of a coast whose government has not agreed to host one.

Everything on the deck is arranged around one number: the interval between launches. The rest of the group - cruiser, destroyers, a submarine, a supply ship - exists to keep that deck operating.
voyages.cite: US Navy fact files; Friedman, *US Aircraft Carriers*.

voyages.name: The Mayflower Autonomous Ship
voyages.text:
No crew, no bridge, no accommodation - a solar-and-diesel trimaran that crossed the Atlantic in 2022 with a rule-based system doing the collision avoidance and a satellite link for supervision.

It broke down twice and had to divert. That is the honest result, and it is still the thing to watch: a hull with nobody in it does not need a hull shaped around people, and almost every constraint on ship design is downstream of the crew.
voyages.cite: IBM/ProMare Mayflower Autonomous Ship, 2022 crossing.

voyages.name: Round the Cape again
voyages.text:
From late 2023, attacks on shipping in the southern Red Sea pushed most container traffic between Asia and Europe back round the Cape of Good Hope - an extra 6,000 km and about ten days.

A canal is not a piece of geography, it is a piece of politics that geography permits; when the politics fails the geography is still there. The Cape route is the default, and Suez is the exception that has to be maintained.
voyages.cite: IMO circulars, 2024; Clarksons Research.
